args.summary: Woman in her early 30s with a continent urinary pouch. She had weeks of worsening difficulty self-catheterizing, so an indwelling pouch catheter was placed. It stopped draining the night before presentation and her urine output fell. She then developed severe lower abdominal pain and worsening shortness of breath, and she arrived with cardiopulmonary decompensation. Stat CT with retrograde contrast into the pouch shows a large left laterodorsal defect in the reservoir, contrast leaking into the peritoneum and free fluid in the abdomen. This confirms an intraperitoneal rupture of the pouch with urinary peritonitis and likely early sepsis. She needs resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency surgical repair.
working_diagnoses: Spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture of continent urinary reservoir (pouch perforation) secondary to catheter drainage failure/overdistension
Urinary peritonitis/urinoma with sepsis or septic shock
Acute kidney injury (obstructive/reabsorptive, pseudo-renal failure from urinary ascites)
Respiratory compromise from abdominal distension/sepsis (abdominal compartment effect, ARDS)
Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis/electrolyte disturbance from urine reabsorption
next_actions: Airway and hemodynamic support, large-bore IV access, balanced crystalloid resuscitation
Stat labs: CBC, BMP/creatinine, venous/arterial blood gas with lactate, coagulation, type and screen
Blood and urine/peritoneal fluid cultures, then empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam)
Decompress pouch/replace catheter if possible as a temporizing measure
Emergency exploratory laparotomy with pouch repair, peritoneal lavage and drainage; ICU postoperatively

args.rationale: This is a woman in her early 30s whose continent urinary pouch ruptured into the peritoneum after her indwelling pouch catheter stopped draining (hpi_002, hpi_003). CT with contrast placed into the pouch showed a large left laterodorsal defect with contrast leaking into the peritoneum (imaging_005). Emergency laparotomy confirmed the rupture, which was repaired. The pouch catheter was fixed in place and a nasogastric tube was inserted (procedure_result_012). She arrived with cardiopulmonary decompensation (physical_exam_004) and a white count of 15.3 (lab_007), so she may have sepsis from urinary peritonitis. She needs close monitoring of breathing and circulation after surgery.
args.followup_or_handoff:
ICU handoff:
- Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours. Narrow it when cultures from surgery or blood come back.
- Monitor breathing, circulation and urine output closely. Watch for sepsis or ARDS.
- Serial labs: CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, blood gas and lactate.
- The pouch catheter must drain continuously. Keep it secured, flush it gently as urology directs, and never clamp it.
- Keep the nasogastric tube on decompression and restart feeding as bowel function returns.
- Watch the surgical drain output. Recheck for a leak with a contrast study of the pouch before removing the catheter, usually around 2-3 weeks.
- Urology to follow her inpatient and to investigate why catheterization became difficult, such as narrowing of the stoma or channel, or stones. Repair any cause they find before she goes back to self-catheterizing.
- Before discharge, teach her how to drain and flush the pouch. Tell her to seek care urgently if drainage fails again.
